Youth Solitary Confinement Harms Mental Health, Rehabilitation
In this op-ed, a Californian who was held in solitary as a teen shares his experience.
By
Sergio Cuevas
September 12, 2023
This piece was published in coordination with
Zealous
, an organization working to amplify the perspective of public defenders.
In the depths of the California Division of Juvenile Justice (DJJ), a place that has gone through numerous
lawsuits
and
name changes
, and where shadows dance on cold concrete walls, solitary confinement — a dark and suffocating world of isolation — was my haunting reality.
The walls of my tiny cell felt like they were closing in, suffocating me both mentally and physically. The days stretched endlessly, with no human contact to hold onto. The deafening silence amplified my thoughts, driving me to the brink of madness.
Isolation became my persecutor, the one companion I could not escape. I tried to keep my mind occupied. Talking to the walls around me was inevitable. If they could respond, I was sure they would tell me stories about the young men who came before me. The ones they had broken before me. I hated the fact that I was stripped of any real opportunities for growth and healing. I felt like a caged animal, trapped in a vicious cycle of despair.
In that barren confinement, there was no hope for change, only a deepening sense of resentment and desperation. In the bleak solitude of my cell, I clung only to memories of what was, and what could’ve been. I was stuck in the past and cast aside by my present situation.
I was a long way from home
—
a distance that felt much longer than the seven-hour drive from where I grew up in Southern California. I felt like a stranger to my family. It had been three years since I had last seen them. Not being able to call my family at the times when I knew they were available was hurting my relationships. I was trying to hold onto the remnants of my family, while fighting to keep my sanity.
The living conditions I experienced denied me even the most basic human rights. I endured unsanitary surroundings and the despair that came with limited exposure to natural light. The state's pursuit of justice is not to reform, it is to punish. It is to try to create a monster out of those who want to try and better their lives. I felt trapped not just by physical walls but by the oppressive weight of a system that discriminates against those people of color like me — a system that is designed to try to break you and bring out the worst in you.
I clung to the hope of alternatives. I was told of
restorative justice
, rehabilitation programs, mental healthcare — even “humane” Scandinavian prisons — that have proven successful. But in my personal experience, there were no actual alternatives offered. I received no rehabilitation. I felt like a body, like a number, like nothing.
Those promised alternatives — the ones that were never actually available to us — offered a glimmer of light amidst the darkness, a chance for true reform and the opportunity to reclaim my life. Instead of solitary, opportunities to be in community with others, to learn and heal, to be treated with dignity. Instead of incarceration, meaningful support for mental health problems, addiction, housing insecurity, unemployment — whatever was needed to help people onto their feet. While I was locked away in the unforgiving grip of solitary confinement, they brought the hope that maybe, one day, there really could be rehabilitation and not just false promises. One day, there could be an end to this
decades-long inhumane practice in California's prisons
.
I had to find my own way to rehabilitation through writing. Writing what I had going on in the moment was like holding a mirror to the inside — to my very soul. It allowed me to be able to know how I was feeling and be in tune with what I had going on. We all have hundreds of inner thoughts that pass through our minds each day, but writing allowed me to put them on paper and see them clearly.
I have now been free for almost two years. I am still working toward redemption every day by paying it forward to others, but that journey should never have been paved with the agonizing solitude that strips away one's humanity. By embracing restorative justice practices, California can extend a lifeline of hope to its incarcerated population. Only then can the walls of solitary confinement crumble, allowing for the healing and transformation that every soul deserves.
I’ve become a stranger among my family
My loved ones say they love
Blood bonds on the brink of snapping
Love gone
where’d it go ?
I’m too far away
you can’t feel me
Time Creates Distance
On the phone you sound close
My minds in the past
Bodies in the Present
Reminiscing
So much
I’m missin
So much time I’ve missed in
I want it, back
Someone give it back
Poem by Sergio Cuevas
